food.text: Around 400 BC, the ancient Iranians invented a special chilled food made of rose water and vermicelli. It was served to royalty in summertime. The ice was mixed with saffron, fruits, and various other flavors.

Irdabama was the most well known and wealthiest businesswoman in the Achaemenid Empire's records at Persepolis. She lived during the reign of Darius the Great, and she mainly dealt in wine and grain. She oversaw her business holdings, production centers and estates.

Irdabama's business records at Persepolis describe how she gave out goods and food rations to her staff. She had her own work force of 480 laborers, mainly centered around what is today Shiraz. Several seals found from her business transactions back up this picture.

According to Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones in 2013, recently uncovered texts in Persepolis indicate that Darius' mother was Irdabama. If so, the wine and grain trader was closely tied to the Achaemenid royal family. The source notes it is not clear exactly who she was, and she may even have been two different women.

art.text: Iran holds the largest concentration of ancient rock reliefs in the Middle East, with 90 panels known in 2007, mostly in Fars, Kurdistan and Khuzestan. Each new empire marked its arrival by carving new panels, often at sites earlier rulers had already used.
art.source_title: Art of rock relief in ancient Iran

art.text: Ancient Persian monuments are notable for a tradition that concentrates on the human figure, mostly male and often royal, and on animals. Court-sponsored art has left many of the most impressive survivals from successive dynasties.

Sasanian architecture reached a peak during the Sasanian era, 224 to 651 CE, when the monarchs lived in splendid palaces such as those at Firouzabad and Bishapur in Fars. The capital city of Ctesiphon, in modern Iraq, was another great showpiece.

Iran/Persia was one of the major centers of ancient music, alongside China, Egypt, Greece, India, Mesopotamia and Rome. Ancient music was frequently characterized by monophony, improvisation, and the dominance of text in musical settings.
Under Darius the Great, the Achaemenids made rock relief an official royal art. Its purpose was mainly funerary.
art.source_title: Art of rock relief in ancient Iran

art.text: The great vaulted hall at Ctesiphon, attributed to the reign of Shapur I, has an arch spanning more than 80 feet and rising 118 feet from the ground. It fascinated architects for centuries and is considered one of the most important pieces of Persian architecture.

From the time of the Achaemenid Empire, the idea of the garden as an earthly paradise spread through Iranian literature to other cultures. The words for paradise in Avestan, Old Persian and Median spread to languages across the world.

Four Achaemenid royal tombs carry relief figures. Only the tomb of Darius the Great is identified by an inscription. The others are believed to belong to Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I and Darius II, and all were looted after Alexander the Great conquered the empire.

The Ziwiye hoard from Kurdistan province, dated to about 700 BC, is a collection of mostly metal objects that probably shows the art of the Persian cities of the period. Delicate Iron Age II metalwork has also been found at Hasanlu.

Persian builders solved the problem of putting a round dome on a square building with the squinch, an arch across each corner that turns the square into an octagon. The dome chamber in the palace at Firouzabad is the earliest surviving example, so Persia is the likely place of invention.

Harps were played in ancient Iran long before the classical age ended. Both vertical and horizontal angular harps are documented at Madaktu, dated to 650 BC, and at Kul-e Fara, dated to 900 to 600 BC. Kul-e Fara has the largest collection of Elamite instruments.

Both vertical and horizontal angular harps have been documented at the archaeological sites of Madaktu (650 BC) and Kul-e Fara (900–600 BC). Kul-e Fara holds the largest collection of Elamite instruments documented.

In 2011 an Italian-Iranian team found the ruins of a monumental gate at Tol-e Ajori, 3 kilometers west of Persepolis. Its glazed brick fragments show the same aurochs and mušḫuššu motifs as the Ishtar Gate. It dates to the mid-to-late sixth century BCE and is a scaled-up version of the Ishtar Gate's inner portion.

The spiral edifice of the Great Mosque of Samarra was based on Persian architecture, such as the spiral tower in the middle of Firouzabad, a former Sasanian capital. Sasanian designs thus travelled well beyond their own borders.

war.text: Cyrus the Great of the Achaemenid dynasty founded the Achaemenid Empire in 550 BC. He defeated Media, Lydia, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and at its peak the empire covered roughly 5.5 million square kilometres, making it the largest of its time.
For all its rapid expansion, the Achaemenid Empire was turned back more than once. It was repulsed from Scythia in 513 BC, from Greece in 492 to 490 BC, and again from Greece in 480 to 479 BC.

Alexander the Great began his campaign against Persia in 334 BC. He defeated Darius III at the Battle of Issus in 333 BC, and after the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC he proclaimed himself king of Asia.

In 499 BC Athens lent support to a revolt in Miletus, which resulted in the sacking of Sardis. This led to an Achaemenid campaign against mainland Greece, known as the Greco-Persian Wars, which lasted through the first half of the 5th century BC.

Xerxes I launched the Second Persian invasion of Greece. At a crucial moment about half of mainland Greece was overrun, including all territory north of the Isthmus of Corinth. Greek victories at Plataea and Salamis then cost Persia its footholds in Europe.
After the death of Darius II in 404 BC, Egypt rebelled under Amyrtaeus. Later pharaohs successfully resisted Persian attempts to reconquer the country until 343 BC, when Artaxerxes III retook Egypt.

Ardashir defeated the last legitimate Parthian king, Artabanos V, in AD 224. Artabanus marched against him a second time that year, and their armies clashed at Hormizdegan, where Artabanus IV was killed. Ardashir was crowned at Ctesiphon as the first king of the new Sasanian Empire, ending the 400-year-old Parthian Empire. He then rapidly extended his territory, demanding fealty from the local princes of Fars and gaining control over Kerman, Isfahan, Susiana, and Mesene.
In the first Persian invasion of Greece, the general Mardonius re-subjugated Thrace and made Macedon a full part of Persia. The war nonetheless ended in defeat for the Persians.

The Persians captured and razed Athens twice, in 480 BC and again in 479 BC. After a string of Greek victories they withdrew, and fighting with the Delian League continued for decades until the peace of Callias in 449 BC.

Artaxerxes II paid the Athenians, Thebans, and Corinthians to fight Sparta, which helped start the Corinthian War. In 387 BC he changed sides and made the Treaty of Antalcidas with Sparta, which returned the Greek cities of Ionia and Aeolis to Persian control.

literature.text: The earliest surviving literary works in an Iranian language are the religious texts of the Avesta, written in Avestan, an Old Iranian sacred language. Its oldest part, the Gathas, is a collection of hymns believed to have been composed by Zoroaster.
Persian literature has roots in Old Persian, which dates back as far as 522 BCE. That is the date of the earliest surviving Achaemenid inscription, the Behistun Inscription.

Parthian, another Middle Iranian language, dates to the first three centuries AD and was likely mutually intelligible with Middle Persian. It was also used in Manichaean texts, and is regarded, along with Middle Persian, as one of the bases of the modern Persian language.

According to legend, Tous, son of Nowzar, founded the city of Tous in Khorassan, next to today's Mashhad. It is said to have been the capital of Parthia and the residence of King Vishtaspa, the first convert to Zoroastrianism.

science.text: Iranian academic centers such as Gundeshapur University, dated to the 3rd century AD, were described as a breeding ground where great scientists from different civilizations came together. These centers built on their predecessors' theories and greatly extended their scientific research over time.

Science during classical antiquity was advanced in several great traditions, and ancient Persia was one of them, alongside Greece, Rome, India, China and Mesoamerica. Together, these civilizations laid the roots of modern sciences.
Some of the earliest records of ancient Iranian medicine appear in the sixth book of the Zend-Avesta. The Vendidad, part of that tradition, devotes most of its last chapters to medicine.

Darius I of Persia had such a great interest in medicine that he re-established the school of medicine in Sais, Egypt, which had previously been destroyed. He restored its books and equipment; his reign falls within the third era of ancient Persian medical history, which began with the Achaemenid dynasty.

The Arabic text Tārīkh al-ḥukamā credits the Academy of Gondishapur with establishing licensure of physicians and proper medical treatment and training. According to this traditional account, the advances of the Sassanid period were continued and expanded during the flourishing of Islamicate sciences at Baghdad.

Modern historians have challenged the story of a medical academy at Gondishapur. Peter Pormann and Emilie Savage-Smith say there is no contemporary pre-Islamic evidence for a medical school or teaching hospital there, and suggest later Islamic historians projected Abbasid-era institutions back onto the Sassanid past.

Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, provides some of the earliest external descriptions of Persian health practices. He says people with conditions resembling leprosy (white sickness) were isolated from the general population to prevent "pollution," which he attributes to a belief that the afflicted had "sinned against the sun." He also describes strict bans on urinating, spitting or washing hands in rivers, because water was revered as sacred. Modern historians caution that his account is framed through Greek cultural norms and the political tensions of the Graeco-Persian Wars.

politics.text: Founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC, the Achaemenid Empire grew out of Persis, where Persian people had settled by the 7th century BC. At its peak it covered roughly 5.5 million square kilometres, making it the largest empire of its time. It stretched from the Balkans and Cyrenaica in the west to the Indus Valley in the east.

In 224, Ardashir I defeated Artabanus IV of Parthia at the Battle of Hormozdgan, where Artabanus met his death, and went on to found the Sasanian Empire. His House of Sasan was determined to restore the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire. It competed far more zealously with Rome than the Arsacids had, sparking a new phase of the Roman–Iranian Wars.

The Parthian Empire, also called the Arsacid Empire, lasted from 247 BC to 224 AD. It was founded by Arsaces I, who led the Parni tribe in conquering Parthia in Iran's northeast. Sitting on the Silk Road between the Roman Empire and Han China, it became a center of trade and commerce.

In autumn 338 BC the eunuch and chiliarch Bagoas, who wanted to be kingmaker, had Artaxerxes III poisoned. Bagoas also murdered most of the king's sons, sparing only Arses and Bisthanes, and put the young Arses on the throne expecting to control him. Arses tried to free himself by having Bagoas poisoned, but failed, and Bagoas had Arses poisoned along with the rest of his family. Bagoas then placed Arses's cousin Darius III on the throne.

After the Spartans under Agesilaus II invaded Asia Minor, Artaxerxes II paid Sparta's enemies, the Athenians, Thebans and Corinthians, to draw the Spartans back to Greek affairs, helping spark the Corinthian War. In 387 BC he betrayed his allies the Spartans and, in the Treaty of Antalcidas, forced them to come to terms. The treaty restored the Greek cities of Ionia and Aeolis to Persian control while giving Sparta dominance on the Greek mainland.

Artaxerxes I weakened Athens by funding its enemies in Greece. This indirectly led the Athenians to move the Delian League's treasury from Delos to the Athenian acropolis. Later sources say the Peace of Callias was agreed in 449 BC, but whether a formal treaty with Persia existed is disputed.

The Medes, in alliance with Babylonia, overthrew the declining Neo-Assyrian Empire by 612 BCE. In 614 BCE they ravaged the territory between Arrapha and Nineveh and captured Tarbiṣu and Assur, and in 612 BCE the combined forces of Cyaxares and Nabopolassar besieged Nineveh for three months until it fell and was sacked. Under Cyaxares the kingdom expanded by subjugating neighboring peoples, including the Persians and Armenians, which led to what is described as the first Iranian empire.

Herodotus's account of a Median Empire is doubted by many historians. They increasingly see the Medes as a loose confederacy that united under one leader only when external powers attacked. Archaeological evidence from sites such as Tepe Nush-i Jan does not match the reconstruction of a Median Empire drawn from classical historians.

Macedonian propaganda later worked to legitimize the conquests of Alexander the Great. It accused Darius III of playing a key role in the murder of Arses, who was portrayed as the last king of the Achaemenid royal house.

Inaros II revolted in Egypt in 460 BC with Athenian allies and defeated the Persian army commanded by the satrap Achaemenes. The Persians retreated to Memphis. The Athenians were finally defeated in 454 BC by an army led by Megabyzus after a two-year siege, and Inaros was captured and carried away to Susa.

Sasanian nobility mixed old Parthian clans, Persian families and families from subjected lands. The Surens, Karens and Varazes held domains that had become part of the Sasanian state as semi-independent states. Their families remained ruling lines in their own right, though subordinate to the shahanshah.

Artaxerxes II is said to have had more than 115 sons from 350 wives. His main wife Stateira was poisoned around 400 BC by his own mother, Parysatis. Another chief wife was Aspasia, a Greek woman of Phocaea.

Artabanus was reportedly the power behind the Persian throne for a few months around 465 BC. According to Aristotle, he was responsible for the death of Crown Prince Darius, then feared Xerxes would seek revenge and assassinated the King. Junianus Justinus instead said Artabanus secretly murdered Xerxes and then accused Darius of parricide, which got Darius executed. Artaxerxes I reportedly slew Artabanus with his own sword, either in battle or by surprise.

philosophy.text: Zoroastrianism was the main religion of Iran through three great empires in a row: the Achaemenid (550-330 BC), the Parthian (247 BC-224 AD) and the Sasanian (224-651 AD). For well over a thousand years it shaped how Iranians thought about the divine.

The Zoroastrian holy book, the Avesta, is dated to between 600 and 1000 BC, though the traditions it rests on are more ancient. It remained the predominant religion of the region until the Muslims conquered Iran.

Persian religious life was not limited to Zoroastrianism. Jewish and Christian communities, including the Church of the East, thrived in the northwest, west and south of Iran. Many people in what was then eastern Iran, such as Bactria and Sogdia, followed Buddhism.

Mithraism was a mystery religion centred on Mithras, a proto-Zoroastrian Persian god. It was widely practised in the Roman Empire from about the 1st to the 4th centuries, carrying a Persian religious idea far from Iran.

Manichaeans believed in a "Father of Greatness", called pid i wuzurgih in Persian, whom they saw as the highest deity, a deity of light. Their 3rd century religion was dualist and may have been influenced by Mandaeism.

In antiquity, Zoroastrianism was not a single uniform faith. It had several variants or denominations that differed slightly by location, ethnic affiliation and historical period. The present-day form is a continuation of the elite form of the Sasanian Empire.

By the end of the third century, Manichaeism reached the attention of the Roman Empire, which viewed it as a "Persian aberration" whose followers were "despicable deviants". Mani's teaching had travelled far beyond the Sasanian world that produced it.

The Avesta contains more than the Gathas. Through the Yashts and Yasna, it mentions polytheism and earlier creeds. Researchers use the Vedas and the Avesta together to uncover early Proto-Indo-Iranian religious beliefs, from which Iranian and Indo-Aryan religions evolved.

culture.text: Zoroastrianism was the main religion of Persia through three great empires: the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BC), the Parthian Empire (247 BC–224 AD) and the Sasanian Empire (224–651 AD). It remained the dominant faith until the Muslim conquest of Iran.

Persia's religious life was not limited to Zoroastrianism. Jewish and Christian communities (the Church of the East) thrived in the north-west, west and south, and a significant number of Iranians followed Buddhism in eastern regions such as Bactria and Sogdia.

Manichaeism was founded by the Iranian prophet Mani (c. 216–274 AD) in the Sasanian Empire. It originated in third century Mesopotamia and spread rapidly from North Africa to Central Asia over the following centuries.

The ancient Iranian prophet Zoroaster reformed the early beliefs of the Iranians into a form of henotheism or monotheism. His hymns, the Gathas, introduced monotheistic ideas to Persia, while the Yashts and Yasna still mention polytheism and earlier creeds.

The word "check" has a Persian root in Old Persian, and such documents were used from Achaemenid times to the end of the Sassanian Empire. A check represented money value for gold, silver and property, and by law people could buy, sell or exchange these documents.
